references.text: The day of preparation has its roots in God's command to prepare before the Sabbath. In [ref:2 Mos 16:23|Exodus 16:23], Moses instructed the people to prepare food on the day before the Sabbath, which laid the foundation for the Jewish 'day of preparation' (paraskeue) that Luke refers to.

The commandment regarding the Sabbath in [ref:2 Mos 20:8-11|Exodus 20:8-11] is the basis for the weekly Sabbath rest that was about to begin when Jesus was buried. The day of preparation existed precisely to ensure everything was ready before the Sabbath started.

In [ref:5 Mos 21:22-23|Deuteronomy 21:22-23], it is commanded that an executed person must not remain hanging on the tree overnight. It was important to take down Jesus' body before the Sabbath began, which explains the haste on the day of preparation.

The parallel account in [ref:Matt 27:57-62|Matthew 27:57-62] tells that it was the day of preparation when Joseph of Arimathea asked for Jesus' body, and that the next day—the Sabbath—the chief priests went to Pilate to secure the tomb.
Mark's parallel account in [ref:Mark 15:42|Mark 15:42] explicitly explains that it was 'the day of preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath,' thus giving the same time reference as Luke.

In [ref:Luk 23:56|Luke 23:56], the thought is completed by stating that the women prepared fragrant spices and oils, but then rested on the Sabbath 'according to the commandment'—a direct result of the Sabbath beginning as described in verse 54.

In [ref:Joh 19:31|John 19:31], John emphasizes that it was the day of preparation, and that the Jews asked Pilate to have their legs broken and their bodies taken down so they would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath.

In [ref:Joh 19:42|John 19:42], John tells that they laid Jesus in a nearby tomb 'because of the Jewish day of preparation,' since the tomb was close by—it was urgent to finish before the Sabbath began.

The expression 'the Sabbath broke in' (ἐπέφωσκεν, literally 'began to shine') refers to the Jewish understanding that a new day begins at sunset. The division of days originates from the creation account: 'and there was evening, and there was morning' ([ref:1 Mos 1:5|Genesis 1:5]).

In [ref:3 Mos 23:32|Leviticus 23:32], the principle is established that a holy day begins 'in the evening, from one evening to the next,' which explains why the Sabbath 'broke in' at sunset on Friday, as Luke describes.
